body_html:
Four days, one convention center, and more handshakes than we could count. The 2026 NMSDC Annual Conference & Exchange took over the Los Angeles Convention Center from October 25 to 28, and our team was there for all of it. Here are our NMSDC 2026 key takeaways, straight from the floor.

This is our honest recap. What was on the official agenda, what we actually learned, the people who made the week worth the flight, and what we think procurement and supplier diversity leaders should do next. Where something comes from NMSDC, we link to it. Where it is our own reading, we say so.

NMSDC 2026 in 60 seconds

What it was: The National Minority Supplier Development Council's flagship event, held October 25 to 28, 2026 at the Los Angeles Convention Center under the theme "Drive Growth. Create Opportunity. Shape the Future of American Prosperity."

Our five biggest takeaways:

  • Certification gets you in the room. Readiness is what wins the contract.
  • The strongest growth stories were partnership stories, not solo bids.
  • AI is now part of supplier conversations, from vendor audits to how buyers find you.
  • Access to capital and global markets came up in session after session.
  • The best opportunities still started with a real conversation in a hallway.

What is the NMSDC Annual Conference and Exchange?

The NMSDC Annual Conference & Exchange is where certified minority business enterprises (MBEs) meet the corporate buyers, procurement teams and supplier diversity leaders who want to work with them. It mixes mainstage keynotes, hands-on Impact Labs, short Spark Sessions, a large exhibit hall called The Exchange, and pre-arranged 1:1 matchmaking.

The scale matters here. In its announcement for this year's event, NMSDC said its certified suppliers generate nearly $600 billion in economic output, support more than 2 million jobs and pay $168 billion in annual wages. That is the economy that showed up in Los Angeles.

For a company like ours, a certified minority- and woman-owned technology firm, it is one of the few rooms where enterprise buyers, government agencies and fellow MBEs are all looking for the same thing: partners they can trust to deliver.

The conference agenda: how NMSDC 2026 unfolded

Here is how the week was laid out on NMSDC's official conference agenda. We have kept it to the moments that shaped the conversations on the floor.

DateWhat was on the official agenda
Sun, Oct 25Registration and invitation-only alumni breakouts, the Opportunity Accelerator 2026 with NMSDC President and CEO Don Cravins, Jr., and the Welcome Reception at the California Science Center.
Mon, Oct 26Mainstage opening, including The State of NMSDC and the American Marketplace, a conversation with former SBA Administrator Isabel Guzman, and a session with Merck's Chief Procurement Officer on the future of supplier development. Then morning Impact Labs, afternoon mainstage sessions on growth, capital and workforce, and the Afternoon Matchmaker.
Tue, Oct 27The Exchange, Marketplace and Matchmakers opened in full, alongside Spark Sessions in The Pitch Room and The Access Point, including the EYE Pitch Competition and a Technology Industry Group session on supplier inclusion and AI.
Wed, Oct 28Fresh Connections and the Members Meeting, a final round of Impact Labs including Power of Partnership: Uniting for Business Growth and Global Impact, and the Awards Ceremony Brunch and Closing Send Off.

Want the short version? Sunday was about getting in the door, Monday set the big picture, Tuesday was for doing business, and Wednesday was for sharpening the plan and celebrating the people behind it.

NMSDC 2026 key takeaways: six lessons we brought home

These are our reading of the week, based on the sessions we attended and the conversations we had. Nobody handed us these on a slide.

1. Certification opens the door. Readiness wins the contract.

Almost every buyer we spoke with said some version of the same thing: being certified gets you considered, but it does not get you selected. The agenda leaned into this, with a Spark Session titled "Turning MBE Certification Into Contract Opportunities" and an Impact Lab from the U.S. Department of Transportation and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services called "Roadmap to Contract Readiness."

The gap between certified and contract-ready usually comes down to the basics. A tight capability statement. Clear proof of past performance. The right identifiers and codes ready to go. Security and compliance answers you can send the same day someone asks.

2. Partnerships beat going it alone

The session that stayed with us most was Power of Partnership: Uniting for Business Growth and Global Impact, an Impact Lab built around how organizations like the Export-Import Bank of the United States help small businesses compete in international markets. The speakers included Nada Allie of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, Terri Batch of Global LA, Pellson Lau of the U.S. Small Business Administration's Office of Manufacturing & Trade, and Simona Racek of Just Down the Street.

Their message was practical. Financing tools, trade programs and the right partners can take a lot of the risk out of growing beyond U.S. borders. The same idea showed up elsewhere on the agenda, in sessions like "Capacity Through Collaboration: How MBEs and Anchors Win as One Team." The pattern is hard to miss. Bigger contracts are increasingly won by teams, not by single suppliers.

Our honest reading: the MBEs growing fastest are not the ones chasing every RFP alone. They are the ones building a bench of partners they can bring into a bid with confidence.

3. AI is now part of the supplier conversation

AI was not a side topic this year. Monday's Impact Labs included "Leading in the AI Era: Five Decisions Every Executive Must Make Today," a session on how physical and IT security now shape vendor audits, and another on what your network, digital footprint and AI say about you before you even walk into a meeting. On Tuesday, the Technology Industry Group asked the direct question: is AI an opportunity or a disruption for supplier inclusion?

For buyers, that means sharper questions about how suppliers protect data and use AI responsibly. For suppliers, it means your security posture and your digital presence are part of your pitch now, whether you planned it or not.

4. Capital and global reach are growth levers, not afterthoughts

Access to capital came up again and again. The afternoon mainstage included "Accelerate Access to Capital: Driving Economic Impact & Empowering Communities," and NMSDC ran an invitation-only "Capital IS Culture LIVE" session through its Capital Readiness Program. Combine that with the export financing discussion in Power of Partnership, and the takeaway is simple. Growth plans that ignore funding and market access tend to stall at the first big contract.

5. Women-owned and minority-owned leadership was impossible to miss

Some of the most energizing conversations we had were with founders who have built serious businesses and now spend their time pulling others up behind them. As a certified minority- and woman-owned business ourselves, that matters to us. Representation is not a talking point at NMSDC. It is the whole room.

6. The hallway is still where deals start

Matchmaking sessions are valuable. But many of the most useful moments of the week happened between them, at the Welcome Reception under the aircraft at the California Science Center, at the kickoff wall, or over coffee before the morning sessions. Structured meetings get you time. Unstructured ones build trust.

The connections that made the week

An event is only as good as the people you meet there. A few conversations we are still thinking about:

Ranjani Mohana

The Certification Lady, R Mo Global Diversity Solutions

Ranjani is a supplier diversity certification specialist and diversity speaker based in California. Through R Mo Global Diversity Solutions, she helps diverse-owned businesses work through certifications such as MBE, DBE and SBA programs, and get ready for government and corporate contracts. If certification paperwork has ever felt like a maze, she is the person who draws the map. It was wonderful to connect with her.

Ann Ramakumaran

Founder and CEO, Ampcus Inc.

We had the pleasure of meeting Anjali "Ann" Ramakumaran, who built Ampcus into a minority- and women-owned technology and consulting firm. Her story is a reminder of what sustained, focused growth looks like for a diverse-owned business.

The Knock Design team

Design and brand partners

A quick hallway hello with the Knock Design team turned into a great conversation about brand, design and how diverse suppliers present themselves to big buyers. Exactly the kind of chance meeting NMSDC is famous for.

The Power of Partnership panel

Impact Lab, October 28

Nada Allie, Terri Batch, Pellson Lau and Simona Racek gave one of the most practical sessions of the week on export financing, trade resources and growing beyond U.S. borders. Pellson Lau and Simona Racek also took the time to meet our team in person, and we are grateful for the conversation.

What procurement and supplier diversity leaders should do next

If you attended, the next two weeks decide whether the conversations turn into anything. If you missed it, the same steps still apply.

  • Follow up within ten days. Send a short note with one clear next step, not a brochure.
  • Ask for readiness, not just certification. Request capability statements, past performance and security documentation up front.
  • Look for teaming, not just vendors. Ask suppliers who they partner with and how they handle work that is bigger than they are.
  • Put AI and security on the first call. How a supplier protects your data now matters as much as what they build.
  • Track Tier 1 and Tier 2 spend from day one. It is far easier to report impact you measured from the start.

If you are building a shortlist of diverse technology partners, our NMSDC 2026 partner shortlist guide walks through the questions worth asking before you sign anything.

Where Procyon fits

Procyon Technostructure is a certified minority- and woman-owned enterprise technology firm with more than 20 years of delivery experience. We help enterprises and public-sector agencies with Salesforce, ServiceNow, AI and machine learning, cloud modernization, cybersecurity and compliance and government solutions.

We went to Los Angeles to listen as much as to talk. What we heard was clear. Buyers want diverse partners who can deliver at enterprise scale, and who make supplier diversity goals easier to hit, not harder.

Every supplier diversity program eventually faces the same question from the finance team: what is this actually worth, and can you prove it? Proving supplier diversity ROI is, at its core, a data problem.

A certified minority business enterprise with a real data and analytics practice can do both, which means the work that proves your program also counts toward it.

Why most diversity ROI claims do not hold up

The usual problem is not a lack of spend, it is a lack of trustworthy measurement. Tier 1 and Tier 2 spend lives in different systems, supplier classifications are inconsistent, and the business outcomes tied to that spend are rarely connected back to it. When the numbers are questioned, the story falls apart. Fixing that is an analytics exercise before it is a reporting one.

title: Dreamforce 2026 Key Takeaways: Seven Agentforce Agents, AIForce & What Enterprises Do Next
excerpt: Seven named agents, a runtime that holds a goal for weeks, and Salesforce data pushed well beyond its own interface. Here is what Dreamforce 2026 actually announced, what it changes for your architecture, and the 90-day plan we would run in your org.
author: Procyon Technostructure
seo_title: Dreamforce 2026 Key Takeaways: AIforce, Koa & Claudeforce
seo_description: Explore the biggest Dreamforce 2026 takeaways, including Salesforce AIforce, Koa, Claudeforce, Agentforce, Data 360 and the future of agentic enterprise.
body_html:
Enterprises have largely settled the question of whether they will use AI. Across three days at Moscone Center the questions that moved were narrower, and far more useful to anyone holding a budget: where should AI operate, how does it reach trustworthy enterprise context, what is it allowed to do, and how does anyone prove it worked.

Procyon's Salesforce and enterprise AI practice was there for all three days. Where a claim below comes from Salesforce we say so. Where it is our reading, we say that too.

Dreamforce 2026 in one minute

Three words summarise what we took away from it.

Placement. Salesforce wants its data and its business capabilities available outside the Salesforce interface, in Slack, in AI assistants, in whatever application your people already have open.

Plumbing. An agent is only as useful as the systems it can reach. Almost every valuable workflow crosses an application boundary, so integration stopped being a supporting act.

Proof. Salesforce put named customer outcomes at the centre of its Agentforce material this year: deflection rates, autonomous resolution, cases handled at volume. That matches what enterprise buyers ask us for, which is a number measured against a baseline rather than a capability shown on stage.

Put those together and the shift is clear enough: the model is becoming the interchangeable part, while trusted data, integration architecture, identity and governance become the hard problems.

What Salesforce actually announced

The headline was AIforce, a live interface layer that makes Salesforce data, workflows, business logic, semantics, permissions, security and governance available inside other AI interfaces. It launched with three surfaces: ClaudeForce, which puts Salesforce inside Claude; Slackforce, which brings Salesforce context into Slack; and Agentforce Coworker, an AI teammate inside Lightning. The banner across Moscone listed five model partners: Anthropic, AWS, Gemini, NVIDIA and OpenAI.

Underneath sits Headless 360, which exposes governed Salesforce capabilities to authorised agents and applications, including over the Model Context Protocol. If you own the architecture, this is the announcement that changes your diagram.

Salesforce also introduced Koa, its first CRM reasoning model, post-trained from NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super on Salesforce data and aimed at multi-step CRM work such as updating an opportunity, routing a case or scheduling a follow-up. On Salesforce's own CRM benchmark it matches or exceeds leading models with three times fewer errors, and both post-training and inference stay inside the Salesforce trust boundary. Pilot customers include Formula 1, Xero, UChicago Medicine and Baxter Credit Union, with general availability expected in winter 2026 in US regions.

Day two was about deployment rather than launch. Slackforce Surfaces reached general availability, alongside Slackbot in Lightning Experience, Big Mode and Slack Code. The Data 360 keynote concentrated on real-time context. AgentExchange opened as a marketplace for prebuilt agents and actions.

Day three belonged to the people who run the platform. The Admin keynote announced Builder Central, a no-code AI workspace that turns a plain-language description into a working app or agent and deploys it to a sandbox in one click, with automated testing and governance rules applied. The beta opened the week of 22 September 2026.

One honest note, because it matters when you read other recaps: Salesforce published no press releases dated 17 September. The third day was enablement and community, not product news. Any recap listing Day 3 announcements is filling a gap that was not there.

Not sure which of these actually applies to your org?

Most of them will not. In 60 minutes we map the Dreamforce announcements onto your specific Salesforce estate and tell you which three are worth your time this quarter.

Book a 60-minute Dreamforce debrief →

The seven named agents, and the runtime underneath them

Salesforce has been a platform for two decades, through Force.com, the API layer and AppExchange. What AIforce and Headless 360 change is where those capabilities get consumed: increasingly from front ends your team does not own or control. That is an identity and governance problem before it is an AI problem, and somebody has to answer, in writing, what an agent can see, what it can change, which systems it reaches through the same session, how every action is logged, and what happens when it is wrong.

Salesforce announced seven job-ready agents on 11 September, four days before the conference opened, and they framed a good deal of what followed. They are also the part of the week most likely to reach a budget conversation, because each one maps to a job somebody in your organisation already owns.

  • Casey resolves customer service issues across voice, SMS, WhatsApp and web chat. Generally available.
  • Paige resolves employee requests across Slack, portals and the tools people already use. Generally available.
  • Carter helps shoppers discover and compare products, answers their questions, and converts with in-chat checkout. Generally available.
  • Piper works across websites and inboxes to engage, qualify and convert inbound leads. Generally available.
  • Fin resolves complex customer experience workflows across every channel. Generally available.
  • Marshall orchestrates end-to-end back-office processes, automating manual work with deterministic execution. Generally available.
  • Hunter works a sales pipeline from research to outreach, collaborating with sellers over weeks and months. In pilot, with general availability expected in November 2026.

Salesforce published customer results alongside them: Anthropic resolving 79 percent of conversations autonomously with Fin, Hibbett covering 90 percent of core shopper journeys with Carter after a six-week launch, Autism Queensland resolving 70 percent of administrative requests with Paige, and Perk building 60 percent of its sales pipeline with Hunter.

Hunter is the one to read twice
Not because outbound sales is the biggest prize. Because Hunter is the one of the seven that cannot live inside a single conversation, so Salesforce had to build something underneath it: a long-horizon runtime that lets an agent, in Salesforce's own words, pursue goals across days and weeks instead of completing only a task or interaction.

Three pieces make that work. Memory preserves context and progress across sessions, so work does not stop when the interaction ends. Durable execution keeps a plan running over time and lets the agent resume or course-correct as circumstances change. Dynamic steering adapts the agent's behaviour to an individual user's feedback. Alongside it, Multi-Agent Orchestration routes work across agents so they operate as one coordinated team.

That is the announcement with the longest shadow, and it is worth being clear about why. A chat agent that gets something wrong produces a bad conversation. An agent that holds a goal for six weeks, resumes after interruptions, coordinates with other agents and adjusts its own plan is a participant in your process. It accumulates state nobody is looking at, acts across systems when no human is watching the thread, and its mistakes compound quietly instead of announcing themselves.

Everything in the rest of this article gets more important, not less, once the agent runs for a month.

The platform is now consumed from outside Salesforce

This is the change with the longest tail. Salesforce has been a platform for two decades, through Force.com, the API layer and AppExchange. What AIforce and Headless 360 change is where those platform capabilities get consumed. A governed Salesforce action can now be invoked from Slack, from Claude or from a custom application, which means increasingly from front ends your team does not own or control.

That is an identity and governance problem before it is an AI problem. If an agent running in Slack or Claude can reach Salesforce, somebody has to answer, in writing:

  • What Salesforce data can this agent see, and under whose permissions?
  • What actions can it take, and which of those need a human to approve?
  • Which systems beyond Salesforce can it reach through that same session?
  • How is every action logged, and who reviews the log?
  • What happens when the agent is wrong, and who notices?

Teams that already run mature enterprise integration and identity practices will find this a natural extension. Teams where Salesforce permissions grew organically over a decade will find it exposes years of accumulated drift. That audit is worth starting now, before an agent does it for you in production.

Context is the moat, not the model

Koa will get the headlines. It is not the part that decides whether any of this works in your organization.

An agent becomes valuable when it understands the customer, the contract, the support history, the entitlement, the business rule and the approval chain around the task in front of it. That understanding does not come from the model. It comes from your data.

Which is why the line that stayed with us was printed on the expo floor rather than delivered from a stage: get your data right to get your AI right. An agent working over clean, connected, governed data automates real work. An agent working over duplicate accounts, half-populated fields, stale integrations and permissions nobody has reviewed since 2019 does not fail safely. It executes the wrong action faster, at scale, with an audit trail saying a human approved the design.

So the question before choosing a model is not which model. It is whether your enterprise context is trustworthy enough for something to act on, across Salesforce, ERP, billing, the customer data platform, the warehouse and whatever industry system actually holds the truth. That is ordinary data engineering and analytics work, and it is the gate.

Agentforce moved from demos to numbers, with one gap

The operational evidence is now substantial. Salesforce reports 3.2 billion Agentic Work Units completed in Q2, up 97 percent on Q1, across more than 30,000 customers in 124 countries.

The named results are more useful than the aggregate:

  • Live Nation at a 95 percent case deflection rate.
  • Xero resolving 62 percent of support cases autonomously across more than 800,000 cases a year.
  • Siemens engaging 100 percent of inbound leads across 132 countries for 18,000 sellers.

Here is the gap, and it is an industry gap rather than a Salesforce one. Containment and deflection are activity measures. They tell you what the agent handled. They do not tell you the fully loaded cost of running it, or what it contributed to margin. Very few published case studies close that loop.

Which means you have to close it yourself, and you can only do that from a baseline recorded before anything is deployed: current volume, current cost to serve, current handling time, current resolution rate, current human effort, and the expected cost to run the agent including inference, integration, monitoring and escalation. Measure the same workflow afterwards on the same definitions. Attach the return to the workflow, never to the platform.

Build the business case before the pilot, not after

We will help your team baseline two or three candidate workflows and size the realistic return, so the pilot has a number to beat rather than a story to tell.

Talk to our enterprise AI team →

Governance has to arrive before agent sprawl

Builder Central lowers the cost of building an agent sharply, and that is precisely why it deserves a governance conversation this quarter rather than next year.

When building an agent required a developer, scarcity did your governance for you. When an administrator can describe one in a sentence and deploy it in a click, that constraint disappears, and organisations can go from three agents to thirty faster than their operating model adapts. The failure mode is the same one Lightning components, flows and integrations all produced: a large estate nobody owns.

Every production agent needs an answer to five questions before it goes live. Who owns it. Who approves what it can access. What it may do without a human. How its performance is monitored. When it gets retired. None of that slows adoption down. It is what lets adoption keep going after the first incident.

The goal is not to govern AI cautiously. It is to make governance scale as fast as building does.

Your 90-day plan after Dreamforce 2026

You do not need to wait for every announced product to reach general availability. Almost all of the preparatory work is available to start now, and most of it is work you would want done regardless.

Days 1 to 30: assess

Identify five to ten workflows that are high volume, measurably painful and owned by somebody who cares. For each one, assess the Salesforce architecture and technical debt behind it, the quality and completeness of the data it depends on, its integration dependencies, and its identity and permission model. Write down explicitly what an agent must never do in that workflow without human approval.

The aim is not a catalogue of every possible AI use case. It is to find the small number where AI would produce a number your CFO recognises.

Days 31 to 60: prove

Pick one to three. Before a line of configuration, assign a business owner, record the baseline, define the success metric, design the human escalation path, and collect the real edge cases from the people who currently do the work. Then build, and test against those edge cases rather than the happy path.

A proof of concept that only proves the technology works has not proved anything commercially interesting. It has to prove a business outcome.

Days 61 to 90: operationalise

Move what worked into controlled production and measure against the original baseline. Review the exceptions, because that is where the next design lives. Then extract the reusable pattern: integration approach, permission model, monitoring, escalation design, documentation.

The objective of the first ninety days is not the maximum number of agents. It is one repeatable enterprise pattern for deploying them safely and profitably. The second workflow should take a third of the time the first one did. If it does not, the pattern is not finished.

Want this as a costed plan for your org?

We will run the assess phase with your team and hand back a prioritised 90-day roadmap with owners, dependencies and effort, whether or not you work with us afterwards.

Request your 90-day roadmap →

Where Procyon fits

Turning any of this into production outcomes takes Salesforce architecture, enterprise integration, data readiness, AI engineering, security, governance and change management working together. That combination is what most teams are missing in one place.

That is the work we do: Salesforce strategy and implementation, Agentforce and enterprise AI, integration and APIs, data engineering and analytics and digital transformation across regulated and complex industries. More than 75 global customers, over 200 enterprise transformation projects and a consistent starting point: find the measurable business problem first, then design the data, integration and technology around solving it.

The question after Dreamforce is no longer whether enterprise AI is coming. It is which process you should improve first, and whether your architecture is ready to carry it.

Salesforce CPQ is now a frozen, end-of-sale product - no new customers, no new features - and all new investment flows into Revenue Cloud Advanced. The catch that changes everything: the move is a reimplementation, not an upgrade. CPQ runs on managed-package custom objects; Revenue Cloud is built on standard platform objects, so pricing logic and bundles are rebuilt rather than copied across. Source: Sweep · Everstage

What Actually Changed

Salesforce CPQ has reached end of sale: no new customers, and no new feature development. Salesforce has not published a hard end-of-life date, so existing customers can keep using and renewing CPQ for now. But make no mistake - it is a frozen product. All new investment flows into Revenue Cloud Advanced (previously Revenue Lifecycle Management), rebuilt on the standard Salesforce platform. The strategic read: this is less a deadline to fear and more a forcing function to modernize quote-to-cash on your own terms.

Why It Is a Reimplementation, Not an Upgrade

This is the single most important thing to understand. Salesforce CPQ is a managed package built on custom objects. Revenue Cloud Advanced is built on standard platform objects. They are different foundations, so there is no one-click migration tool that lifts your configuration across.

Salesforce CPQ Revenue Cloud Advanced
Managed package Native platform
Custom objects Standard platform objects
Frozen (end of sale) Active roadmap and investment
Familiar to your admins New model and skills to learn

Your product catalog, pricing rules, discount logic, and bundle structures are rebuilt and re-tested against the new model, not copied. That is more work than an upgrade - but it is also a rare chance to retire years of accumulated CPQ complexity instead of carrying it forward.

What a Migration Involves

  1. Discovery and rationalization: inventory every product, rule, and bundle - and decide what still earns its place. Most CPQ orgs carry logic no one uses.

  2. Data cleanup: clean the product and pricing data before it moves. Debt migrated is debt multiplied.

  3. Rebuild on standard objects: model products, pricing, and bundles in Revenue Cloud Advanced using upgrade-safe patterns.

  4. Integration and quote-to-cash: reconnect CRM, ERP, billing, and any downstream systems.

  5. Test against real deals: validate pricing and bundles with real, messy quote scenarios, not just clean samples.

  6. Phased cutover and enablement: roll out with training so RevOps and sales adopt the new model.

THE MOST COMMON MISTAKE

Treating the move as a like-for-like rebuild. Teams that simply recreate their old CPQ configuration in the new platform inherit all of its complexity and miss the one opportunity a reimplementation offers: to simplify the pricing model itself.

Migrate Now or Wait?

If your CPQ works and you have no urgent driver, you are not forced to move today - but a reimplementation needs exactly what waiting consumes: time. The pragmatic path for most teams is to start discovery and data cleanup early so the build can happen on your schedule, with a rationalized catalog, rather than under pressure later. A CPQ-to-Revenue-Cloud move is a natural part of a broader application modernization plan, and it lives inside our Salesforce practice.

excerpt: Salesforce technical debt rarely announces itself. It shows up as slower releases, brittle automation, and a team afraid to touch production.  Slug (URL): /blog/  Focus Keyword:  Category:   Tags: Salesforce, technical debt, Apex, Flow, clean core, refactoring

seo_description: The five most common Salesforce technical debt patterns that slow US teams down - and a practical, prioritized way to fix each one.

faqs.a: It is the accumulated cost of past shortcuts and unmanaged growth in your org - automation sprawl, untested Apex, unused fields, hardcoded logic, and manual releases - that slows delivery and makes every change riskier. It is the gap between how the org is built today and how it would need to be built to change safely and quickly.
faqs.q: What is Salesforce technical debt?

faqs.a: Watch for the symptoms: releases taking longer than they used to, automation breaking when you change something unrelated, and a team reluctant to touch production. Those are signs of one or more of the five common debt patterns, and a structured org review can confirm which.
faqs.q: How do I know if my Salesforce org has technical debt?

faqs.a: Yes, significantly. An AI agent acts on your data and through your automation, so it inherits every underlying flaw. Orgs with unmanaged debt often discover mid-project that an agent cannot be trusted because the foundation cannot be trusted, which is why remediation and AI initiatives should be sequenced together.

faqs.a: Foundational fixes like source control and a release pipeline can be stood up in weeks. Full remediation of automation, code, and data debt is best done incrementally over one to two quarters, cleaning each area as you touch it for other work rather than as a single large project.
faqs.q: How long does it take to reduce Salesforce technical debt?

body_html:
Salesforce technical debt is the accumulated cost of past shortcuts, unmanaged growth, and expedient decisions in your org that now slow every change and raise the risk of every release. It does not appear on a balance sheet, but your delivery team pays interest on it in every sprint. This guide breaks down the five patterns that account for most enterprise Salesforce debt, what each one costs the business, and a prioritized way to pay it down without stalling your roadmap.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Most Salesforce technical debt falls into five patterns: automation sprawl, untested or untrusted Apex, field and object bloat, hardcoded logic and IDs, and the absence of source control and a release process. Each degrades delivery speed and raises operational risk, and all five compound when left unmanaged. The highest-leverage first move is almost always to establish version control and a repeatable release pipeline, because it makes every other fix safer. You do not need zero debt; you need debt you have chosen and can see, rather than debt that quietly runs your roadmap.

What Salesforce technical debt actually is

Technical debt is not the same as bad work. It is the gap between how your org is built today and how it would need to be built to change safely and quickly. Some of that gap is deliberate - a reasonable shortcut taken to hit a deadline. Some of it is accidental - the residue of many admins and developers making locally sensible choices over years, with no one owning the whole picture. Either way, the interest is real: releases take longer, changes break unrelated features, and the team grows cautious around a system that has become hard to reason about. On Salesforce specifically, debt accumulates faster than on many platforms because the barrier to change is so low. A business user can create a field, an admin can add a flow, and a developer can write a trigger, all without a shared design. That accessibility is a strength, but without governance it produces exactly the sprawl described below.

The business impact: why leaders should care

For a CIO or Salesforce leader, technical debt is not an engineering vanity concern - it is a direct tax on the business. It shows up in four places that executives feel:

  • Slower time to market. Every new capability takes longer to ship because the org is harder to change safely.
  • Higher operational risk. Brittle automation and untested code mean routine changes can trigger outages that reach customers.
  • Rising cost to run. More admin hours go to firefighting and workarounds instead of new value.
  • Blocked innovation. Debt-laden orgs struggle to adopt new platform capabilities, and this is now acute: an AI agent or an integration built on messy data and tangled automation inherits every underlying flaw.

That last point matters more in 2026 than ever. Gartner has estimated that poor data quality costs organizations an average of $12.9 million per year , and as enterprises layer AI agents onto Salesforce, the foundation's condition becomes the ceiling on what those agents can safely do.

See where your org's technical debt is hiding

A structured review surfaces the patterns below in your specific org and ranks them by delivery risk - so you fix what actually slows you down first.

Request a Salesforce Org Review

The 5 Salesforce technical debt patterns

Each pattern has a recognizable symptom, a root cause, a business cost, and a fix. Learn the tells and you can name the debt before it compounds.

1
Automation sprawl
Symptom: one object is touched by a tangle of Workflow Rules, Process Builder, and overlapping Flows built by different people over years, so a change in one has unpredictable effects. Root cause: no per-object automation design or ownership. Fix: consolidate onto Flow, map every trigger per object, and retire redundant automation deliberately.
2
Apex without trust
Symptom: Apex that meets the coverage requirement but whose tests assert nothing meaningful, so nobody trusts a deploy. Root cause: tests written to pass a gate, not to verify behavior. Fix: treat tests as behavior specifications, refactor the riskiest classes first, and write assertions that would actually catch a regression.
3
Field and object bloat
Symptom: hundreds of custom fields, many unused, duplicated, or half-populated, slowing every page, report, and automation. Root cause: no governance gate on new fields. Fix: audit field usage, deprecate the dead ones on a schedule, and require justification before new fields are added.
4
Hardcoded logic and IDs
Symptom: record IDs, org URLs, and business rules baked into code and formulas, so every environment move or business change becomes a manual hunt. Root cause: convenience under deadline pressure. Fix: externalize logic to Custom Metadata Types and Custom Settings so it is configurable, not compiled.
5
No source control or release process
Symptom: changes made directly in production, no clear history of who changed what, deployments done by hand. Root cause: the org grew faster than its engineering discipline. Fix: adopt version control and a defined CI/CD release pipeline. This is the single highest-leverage change most Salesforce teams can make.

How the patterns reinforce each other

These are rarely isolated. Automation sprawl is far more dangerous without source control, because you cannot see what changed or roll it back. Field bloat makes untested Apex riskier, because more surface area means more ways for an unasserted test to hide a defect. Hardcoded IDs turn every deployment into a manual, error-prone event precisely when you have no pipeline to catch mistakes. This is why debt compounds: each pattern raises the cost and risk of living with the others.

How to prioritize the fixes

You cannot fix all five at once, and trying usually stalls the roadmap. Sequence by risk and leverage rather than by which bothers you most.

  1. Establish the release process first (pattern 5). Source control and a repeatable deploy make every other fix safer and reversible. It is the foundation the rest stand on.
  2. Stabilize whatever is actively causing incidents. If automation sprawl is breaking things monthly, it jumps the queue regardless of the ideal order - stop the bleeding.
  3. Address bloat and hardcoding incrementally. Clean each area as you touch it for feature work, rather than launching a big-bang cleanup that competes with delivery.
  4. Make prevention permanent. A governance gate for new fields and automation stops the debt you just cleared from silently rebuilding.
FIX DEBT WHERE YOU ALREADY ARE

The most sustainable way to pay down Salesforce debt is not a dedicated cleanup project that competes with the roadmap. It is a standing rule that any area you touch for feature work gets left cleaner than you found it. This spreads the cost across normal delivery and concentrates it on the parts of the org that are actually active, which is where the interest is highest.

A realistic scenario

Consider a mid-market company whose Salesforce releases had slipped from weekly to monthly. The team blamed complexity, but the root cause was concrete: three generations of automation on the Opportunity object, no source control, and a test suite that asserted nothing. Every deploy was a manual, anxious event. The fix was sequenced, not heroic. First, version control and a simple CI pipeline, so changes were visible and reversible. Then the Opportunity automation was mapped and consolidated onto a single Flow. Only then did the team refactor the riskiest Apex with real assertions. Within a quarter, releases returned to weekly - not because anyone worked harder, but because the org stopped fighting back.

Not sure which debt to fix first?

We assess your org against all five patterns and hand you a prioritized remediation plan - sequenced so the earliest fixes make the later ones safer and faster.

Discuss Your Salesforce Technical Debt

When your internal team can fix it, and when to bring in a partner

Not every debt problem needs outside help. Use this as a rough decision guide:

Situation Who should lead
You have a strong admin/dev team and the debt is contained to one area Internal team, with a clear plan
You need to stand up source control and CI/CD for the first time Partner accelerates it and transfers the practice to your team
Automation sprawl spans many objects and owners Partner - untangling safely needs architecture experience
Debt is blocking an AI or integration initiative on a deadline Partner - the remediation and the initiative must be sequenced together
You lack the bandwidth to remediate while keeping the lights on Partner - so delivery does not stall during cleanup

The honest tell is rarely capability - it is bandwidth and breadth. A capable internal team can fix a contained problem well; a partner earns its place when the debt is cross-cutting, the discipline is new, or the clock is running on something that depends on a clean foundation.

The risk of delaying

Debt is not static - it accrues interest. Every quarter you defer the foundational fixes, more automation, fields, and code get built on the unstable base, making the eventual remediation larger and riskier. The most expensive version of this problem is the one discovered mid-way through a high-visibility AI or integration project, when the team learns that the agent cannot be trusted because the data and automation underneath it cannot be trusted. Paying down foundational debt on your own schedule is always cheaper than paying it down under the pressure of a stalled strategic initiative.

Key takeaways

  • Salesforce technical debt is a direct tax on delivery speed and operational risk, not an abstract engineering concern.
  • Five patterns account for most of it: automation sprawl, untrusted Apex, field and object bloat, hardcoded logic, and no release process.
  • The patterns compound, so fixing the foundation - source control and a release pipeline - first makes every other fix safer.
  • Pay debt down incrementally as you touch each area, and add governance gates so it does not silently rebuild.
  • Bring in a partner when the debt is cross-cutting, the engineering discipline is new, or it is blocking a strategic initiative on a deadline.

body_html:
A Salesforce org health check is a structured review of your org's data, automation, security, architecture, and adoption to find the risks and inefficiencies that are quietly slowing you down. Salesforce problems rarely arrive as one dramatic failure. They accumulate: a broken flow here, a duplicate-riddled report there, a feature nobody uses. Individually easy to ignore, together they become the reason projects stall and users lose trust. These are the ten signs it is time for an expert review.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

You likely need a Salesforce org health check when you see recurring symptoms across four areas: unreliable data, brittle or unpredictable automation, security and access drift, and falling user adoption. A tenth and increasingly common trigger is a stalled AI or Agentforce initiative that cannot proceed because the underlying org is not ready. A health check examines data quality, automation, security model, technical debt, integration, and adoption, then returns a prioritized remediation plan. The goal is not a report - it is a ranked list of what to fix, in what order, and why.

What a Salesforce org health check actually is

It is a systematic assessment of the state of your org, conducted against known best practices and your own business goals. A good health check does not just list problems; it explains their business impact, ranks them by risk and effort, and recommends a sequence. It typically covers data quality, automation and code, the security and sharing model, technical debt, integrations, licensing and cost efficiency, and user adoption. The output is a decision tool for leadership, not a technical audit for its own sake.

Why it matters to the business

An unhealthy org is a slow, risky, and expensive org. It ships change more slowly, breaks more often, costs more to run, and blocks the initiatives that depend on it. Data is where this bites hardest: Gartner has estimated poor data quality costs organizations an average of $12.9 million per year , and in Salesforce that cost surfaces as wrong reports, misfired automation, and AI that cannot be trusted. As enterprises move to layer Agentforce and analytics onto their CRM, org health stops being hygiene and becomes the precondition for the roadmap.

Suspect your org needs a closer look?

A structured review pinpoints the data, automation, and security issues holding your org back - and ranks them so you know exactly what to fix first.

The 10 signs you need an expert review

Any one of these is worth attention. Several together mean the interest on your org's accumulated problems is coming due.

1
Reports and dashboards contradict each other
Two dashboards answer the same question differently, and leadership no longer trusts the numbers. It signals data quality and definition problems beneath the reporting layer.
2
Automation breaks when you change something unrelated
A small edit triggers failures elsewhere. This is the classic tell of automation sprawl - overlapping flows and rules with no clear ownership.
3
Releases keep slowing down
Changes that used to take days now take weeks, and every deploy feels risky. It points to missing source control, weak testing, and accumulated technical debt.
4
Duplicate and incomplete records are everywhere
Sales and service teams waste time reconciling records, and campaigns hit the wrong contacts. A sign of missing deduplication and data governance.
5
Users are working around Salesforce
Teams keep parallel spreadsheets or skip steps. Low adoption usually means the org has drifted away from how people actually work.
6
Nobody can explain how a key process works
Critical automation exists, but no one fully understands it, and the person who built it has left. This is undocumented, high-risk complexity.
7
Your security and sharing model has drifted
Permissions have accreted over years, ex-employees may retain access, and nobody is confident who can see what. A compliance and risk exposure.
8
Integrations fail silently
Data stops syncing between Salesforce and other systems, and you find out from a customer, not an alert. It indicates fragile, unsupported integration.
9
Costs are rising without clear value
Licenses, storage, and add-ons grow, but the value is unclear and unused features abound. A sign of licensing and cost inefficiency worth auditing.
10
An AI or Agentforce project has stalled
You tried to launch an agent or advanced analytics and hit a wall. Almost always the org - its data and automation - was not ready for what you asked it to.

What an experienced reviewer examines

Automation & code Flows, Apex, test coverage, ownership Fragility and delivery risk
Security model Profiles, permission sets, sharing, access reviews Compliance and exposure gaps
Technical debt Source control, release process, hardcoding How safely the org can change
Integration Sync reliability, monitoring, API governance Hidden failure points
Adoption & cost Usage, unused licenses, feature fit Wasted spend and workflow drift

Can we do a health check ourselves, or do we need an expert?

A strong internal admin team can and should monitor org health continuously, and for a contained, well-understood org, an internal review may be enough. An external expert earns their place in three situations: when you need an objective view that internal politics or familiarity can obscure, when the issues span data, architecture, and security in ways that need cross-domain experience to untangle, or when a health check is the first step before a major initiative like Agentforce, where being wrong about readiness is expensive. The value of an outside reviewer is pattern recognition: they have seen how these symptoms resolve across many orgs and can tell you which are cosmetic and which are load-bearing.

The cost of waiting

Ignoring the signs does not hold the problem steady - it lets it compound. Unmanaged automation grows more tangled, data drifts further, and more work gets built on the shaky foundation, making eventual remediation larger. The most expensive path is to discover the org's condition mid-way through a strategic project, when a stalled Agentforce launch or a failed integration forces an emergency review under deadline pressure. A planned health check on your own schedule is far cheaper than a forced one during a crisis.

  • A Salesforce org health check is a structured review of data, automation, security, technical debt, integration, and adoption.
  • Watch for the ten signs - contradictory reports, brittle automation, slowing releases, duplicate data, workarounds, undocumented processes, security drift, silent integration failures, rising cost, and stalled AI.

title: Headless Salesforce: The API-First Architecture CIOs Need
excerpt: Your customers meet your brand in a dozen places Salesforce does not render. API-first architecture is how the platform keeps up.
author: Siva
seo_title: Headless Salesforce: The API-First Architecture Guide
seo_description: What headless, API-first Salesforce architecture means, when CIOs need it, and how to decouple experience from platform without losing governance.

faqs.a: Headless Salesforce means using Salesforce as the system of record and business-logic engine while delivering the user experience through separate front ends - web, mobile, portals, kiosks, or partner apps - that talk to Salesforce through APIs rather than its built-in UI. The head (presentation) is decoupled from the body (data and logic).
faqs.q: What does headless Salesforce mean?

faqs.a: They are closely related but not identical. API-first is a design discipline: every capability is exposed as a well-governed API before a UI is built on top. Headless is an architectural outcome that API-first enables, where experiences are delivered independently of the platform's native interface.
faqs.q: Is API-first the same as headless?

faqs.a: Consider it when you need to serve multiple front ends, deliver custom or high-performance customer experiences, integrate Salesforce data into other systems and AI agents, or avoid locking business logic inside a single UI. It is overkill for a straightforward internal CRM with one interface.
faqs.q: When should a CIO consider headless Salesforce?

body_html:
Headless Salesforce is an architecture that separates Salesforce as the governed system of record - its data, logic, and security - from the interfaces your users and customers actually touch. Instead of Salesforce rendering the screen, it exposes its capabilities as APIs that any front end can consume. For enterprises whose experiences increasingly live outside the platform, this shift is the difference between Salesforce keeping up and Salesforce becoming a bottleneck.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Traditional Salesforce architecture assumes the platform renders the user interface. Headless, or API-first, architecture drops that assumption: Salesforce becomes the governed core, and web apps, mobile apps, portals, kiosks, and voice assistants all read and write through APIs. You need it when customers meet your brand across many channels Salesforce does not natively render, when you need one source of truth across those surfaces, or when front-end teams must ship independently of platform release cycles. The main risk is governance - decoupling the experience can quietly decouple control - which is why the API layer, often managed with MuleSoft, must be designed as a product, not bolted on.

What 'headless' actually means

Borrowed from the content-management world, 'headless' separates the body from the head. The body is Salesforce as the system of record: customer, order, and case data, business logic, and the security and governance around it. The head is the interface a user touches. In a traditional setup, Salesforce draws that interface. In a headless setup, Salesforce exposes its capabilities through APIs, and any number of front ends consume them - all reading from and writing to one governed core. 'API-first' is the discipline that makes headless work. It means you design those APIs deliberately, as a durable product with versioning, documentation, and governance, rather than exposing endpoints ad hoc whenever a new channel needs data. The distinction matters: headless without API-first discipline is just a pile of integrations waiting to become the next generation of technical debt.

Why this matters now

Customer expectations have outrun the single-screen model. A modern enterprise customer might start on a marketing site, continue in a mobile app, get service through a chat assistant, and complete a purchase in an embedded checkout - none of which Salesforce renders. If each of those surfaces holds its own copy of customer data, you get drift, inconsistency, and a support team reconciling versions of the truth. API-first architecture puts one governed core behind all of them, so the customer sees a consistent brand and your teams work from one record.

Weighing a move to API-first Salesforce?

A short architecture session maps your channels and data flows and tells you honestly whether headless is justified for your estate - or whether a simpler path gets you there.

Book a Salesforce Architecture Session

When do you actually need headless Salesforce?

Headless is a serious architectural commitment, not a default. The signals that justify it are specific:

  • Customers interact with you across many channels that Salesforce does not natively render - mobile apps, partner portals, kiosks, IoT, or voice.
  • You need a consistent experience and one source of truth across web, mobile, and partner surfaces.
  • Product and engineering teams need to move at their own pace on the front end without waiting on platform release cycles.
  • You are building composable architecture, where best-of-breed systems each do one job well and are wired together deliberately.
  • You are exposing Salesforce data to AI agents or external applications that need programmatic, governed access.

If none of these are true - if your users live inside Salesforce and the standard Lightning experience serves them well - headless adds complexity you do not need. The architecture earns its cost only when the experience genuinely has to live outside the platform. An honest partner will tell you when you do not need it.

Headless vs traditional Salesforce: an honest comparison

Consideration Traditional (Salesforce renders UI) Headless (API-first)
Time to a standard UI Fast - use what ships Slower - you build the front end
Multichannel experience Constrained to platform surfaces Consistent across any channel
Front-end flexibility Bounded by the platform Full control of the experience
Engineering skill required Admin and declarative-heavy Front-end and integration engineering
Governance Centralized by default Must be designed into the API layer
Total cost of ownership Lower for standard use Higher, justified by multichannel value
Best fit Internal users, standard workflows Customer-facing, multichannel, composable

The architecture: how the pieces fit

A well-designed API-first Salesforce estate has three layers. The system of record is Salesforce, holding data, business logic, and security. The API and integration layer exposes that core as governed, versioned services - this is where an integration platform such as MuleSoft typically lives, providing the API management, security, and orchestration that the platform used to provide implicitly. The experience layer is the set of front ends - web, mobile, portal, assistant - each consuming the APIs without needing to know how the core is built. The value of this separation is that any layer can change without forcing a change in the others, as long as the API contract holds.

THE GOVERNANCE YOU MUST NOT LOSE
The central risk in going headless is that decoupling the experience quietly decouples the governance too. When many front ends hit your core through APIs, those APIs become the control plane - so security, rate limiting, versioning, and access policy have to be designed into the API layer, not assumed. This is exactly where a managed integration platform like MuleSoft earns its place: it restores the governance the monolithic platform used to provide for free. Skip this and you trade a rigid but safe architecture for a flexible but ungoverned one, which is a worse place to be.

Common failure patterns

Headless projects fail in predictable ways. Knowing them is half the defense:

  • Going headless everywhere at once. A full re-architecture in one program is high-risk and usually stalls. Decouple one experience at a time.
  • Treating APIs as an afterthought. Endpoints built ad hoc per channel become unmanageable. Design the API as a versioned product from the start.
  • Losing the governance thread. Without deliberate API security and access control, you expose the core more broadly than anyone intended.
  • Underestimating the front-end investment. You are now responsible for building and maintaining experiences the platform used to give you. Budget for it.

Want an architecture that decouples experience without losing control?

We design API-first Salesforce estates with governance built into the API layer - and we start with your highest-value channel, not a risky big-bang rebuild.

Book a Salesforce Architecture Session

How to get there without a big bang

You do not have to go headless everywhere at once, and you should not. The pragmatic path is incremental:

  1. Pick the highest-value external experience. Usually a customer-facing channel where consistency and speed matter most.
  2. Design the APIs it needs as a product. Versioned, documented, secured, and governed from day one.
  3. Stand up the governance layer. Put API management and security in place before you expose the core widely.
  4. Prove the model, then extend. Once one experience runs cleanly on the API-first core, add the next, reusing the discipline you built.

Enterprises that try to re-architect the whole estate in one program usually stall; those that decouple one experience at a time build the API discipline as they go and keep delivering value throughout.

When internal teams can lead, and when to bring in a partner

If you have strong integration architects and front-end engineers and a clear API governance model already, an internal team can lead a headless initiative. Most enterprises bring in a partner for one of three reasons: to establish the API governance and MuleSoft layer correctly the first time, to design the decoupling sequence so it delivers value early instead of stalling, or to avoid re-learning failure patterns that an experienced team has already seen. The decision is less about whether your team is capable and more about whether this is your first time doing it at enterprise scale.

  • Headless Salesforce separates the governed core (data, logic, security) from the interfaces users touch, exposing capabilities as APIs.
  • You need it when experiences live across many channels Salesforce does not render, or when front-end teams must move independently.
  • The main risk is losing governance: security and access control must be designed into the API layer, often with MuleSoft.
  • Adopt it incrementally - one high-value experience at a time - rather than in a single big-bang re-architecture.
  • If your users live inside Salesforce and the standard UI serves them, headless adds needless cost.

title: Cloud Migration Strategy: The 6 R's Framework for US Enterprises
excerpt: Not every workload should move to the cloud the same way. The 6 R's framework helps you decide, application by application, what to do and why.
author: John
seo_title: Cloud Migration Strategy: The 6 R's Framework Guide
seo_description: A practical guide to the 6 R's of cloud migration - rehost, replatform, refactor and more - so US enterprises pick the right path per workload.

faqs.a: Rehost (lift and shift), replatform (lift and reshape), refactor (re-architect), repurchase (move to SaaS), retire (decommission), and retain (keep on-premises for now). Each workload is assigned one strategy based on its value, complexity, and constraints.
faqs.q: What are the 6 R's of cloud migration?

faqs.a: Rehosting is fast and low-risk and is the right call for many workloads. But rehosting everything leaves cloud-native benefits on the table. The strongest strategies mix rehosting with selective replatforming and refactoring where the payoff is real.
faqs.q: Is lift and shift a good cloud migration strategy?

faqs.a: Start with a portfolio assessment that scores each workload on business value, technical complexity, and constraints such as compliance and dependencies. High-value, high-change applications justify refactoring; stable commodity workloads favor rehosting or repurchasing; low-value applications are candidates to retire.
faqs.q: How do I decide which strategy to use for each application?

body_html:
The fastest way to a disappointing cloud program is to treat migration as a single decision. 'We are moving to the cloud' is not a strategy - it is a headline. The real work is deciding, application by application, how each workload should move, and being honest that some of them should not move at all yet. The 6 R's framework is the industry-standard way to make those calls consistently across a portfolio. Here is how each option works, when to use it, and how to avoid the trap of lifting and shifting everything and calling it transformation.

WHY THE APPROACH MATTERS

MuleSoft's 2026 benchmark shows 86% of leaders still fighting integration complexity - much of it created when workloads move to the cloud without a plan. A workload that was inefficient on-premises is simply inefficient in the cloud, now with a monthly bill attached. The 6 R's exist so you can be deliberate. Source: MuleSoft 2026

Why 'Lift and Shift Everything' Fails Quietly

Rehosting an entire estate to the cloud is fast, and it feels like progress. But as a whole-portfolio strategy it delivers a data center in someone else's building. Lift and shift is a legitimate tactic for parts of a portfolio; applied to everything, it just relocates your inefficiency. The 6 R's exist so you can decide deliberately instead.

The 6 R's, Explained

1
Rehost (lift and shift)

Move the workload as-is. Fast and low-risk. Best for stable applications, tight timelines, or a first step you will optimize later.

2
Replatform (lift and reshape)

Make targeted improvements during the move - a managed database, autoscaling, container packaging - without a full rewrite. Best when small changes unlock outsized operational gains.

3
Refactor (re-architect)

Rebuild the application to be cloud-native. Highest effort, highest payoff. Reserve it for high-value, high-change applications where scalability is a genuine differentiator.

4
Repurchase (move to SaaS)

Replace a custom or legacy application with a commercial subscription product. Best for commodity functions where a mature SaaS option does the job better.

5
Retire (decommission)

Turn it off. Most portfolios carry applications no one truly uses. Migration is the perfect moment to find and retire them.

6
Retain (keep for now)

Some workloads should stay on-premises due to compliance, latency, or dependencies. Retaining deliberately is a decision; retaining by neglect is not.

How to Assign an R to Each Workload

Workload profile

Usual best fit

Stable, commodity, low change

Rehost or Repurchase

Operationally painful but valuable

Replatform

Strategic, differentiating, high change

Refactor

Redundant or unused

Retire

Compliance or latency bound

Retain (revisit later)

Migration rarely stands alone - it usually sits inside a broader modernization effort. See how it connects to our enterprise application modernization approach and our cloud transformation services.

START WITH A PORTFOLIO ASSESSMENT

You cannot assign the 6 R's from intuition. Score every application on business value, technical complexity, and constraints such as compliance and dependencies. The assessment is what turns 'move to the cloud' into a defensible, sequenced plan.

Sequencing the Program

  1. Assess the portfolio and assign an R to every workload.

  2. Start with quick, low-risk wins (rehost and retire) to build momentum and free capacity.

  3. Replatform the operationally painful workloads next for fast operational relief.

  4. Refactor the strategic few deliberately, with clear success metrics.

  5. Establish landing-zone governance early - security, identity, and monitoring - so growth stays controlled.

THE MOST COMMON MISTAKE

Teams refactor the wrong applications first - usually the ones the loudest engineer finds interesting, not the ones the business depends on. Let the portfolio assessment, not enthusiasm, drive sequence.

body_html:
Agentforce is Salesforce's platform for building AI agents that can reason over your business data, decide what to do, and take real actions inside Salesforce, within guardrails you define. The one word that separates it from the chatbots you have already tried is act. A chatbot answers a question; an Agentforce agent looks up the order, checks the policy, issues the refund, updates the record, and escalates to a human only when it reaches the edge of what it is allowed to do.

How Agentforce differs from a chatbot or copilot

These three terms get blended in marketing, but the difference is practical and it matters the moment you scope a project.

Chatbot Copilot Agent (Agentforce)
What it does Answers scripted questions Suggests; a human acts Takes the action itself
Autonomy None Human in the loop Autonomous within guardrails
Grounded in your data Often no Yes Yes, via Data Cloud
Best for FAQs Assisting a human agent Resolving whole tasks end to end

Because an agent acts rather than answers, the stakes of bad data rise sharply. A chatbot with a wrong answer is annoying; an agent that acts on a duplicate or stale record does real damage. That is why the rest of this guide keeps coming back to data and guardrails.

How an Agentforce agent actually works

Under the hood, every agent is made of four moving parts. Understanding them is enough to hold your own in any vendor conversation:

  • Topics - the bounded jobs the agent may handle (order status, returns, scheduling). Scope is a feature, not a limitation.

  • Actions - the specific things it can do: query a record, call an API, create a case, trigger a Flow. Each is defined and permissioned.

  • Guardrails - the rules that stop it doing something it technically could, such as requiring approval before a refund.

  • Grounding data - the trusted data it reasons over, usually unified through Data Cloud. An agent is only as good as the data beneath it.

What can Agentforce do? Real use cases

The use cases that pay off first share a pattern: high volume, tightly bounded, and measurable. A few that are working today:

  • Service: resolving tier-1 cases such as order status and returns, so human agents handle the complex ones.

  • Sales: qualifying inbound leads and booking meetings around the clock.

  • Internal ops: an HR or IT service desk that answers from your own knowledge with clean escalation.

  • Commerce: answering product questions and guiding buyers on your storefront.

For context on scale: Salesforce reports Agentforce has passed $1 billion in annual recurring revenue, one of its fastest-growing products ever - a sign the technology has moved from demo to daily operations.

What it takes to run Agentforce well

Agentforce lowers the cost of building AI, but it does not remove three requirements that decide whether it works in production: clean, unified data in the objects the agent touches; a clearly defined scope with guardrails; and a named owner with a success metric agreed before launch. Skip these and you join the roughly 40% of agentic projects that Gartner expects to be cancelled by 2027 - almost always for weak foundations, not weak AI.

Agentforce will be the star of Dreamforce 2026 - in the keynote, on the show floor, and in nearly every partner conversation. The demos will be flawless. That is exactly the problem. A great demo shows what is possible in a clean sandbox; it says nothing about your org, your data, or your governance. Here is how to see past the polish: what to look for in the Agentforce sessions, and the hard questions that separate a production-ready plan from a slide.

What to look for in the Agentforce sessions

  • How the agent is grounded: is it reasoning over unified, trustworthy data, or a curated sandbox? Ask what happens with messy real data.

  • Where the guardrails are: a good session shows what the agent will not do and how it escalates, not just its wins.

  • The path to production: look for how a demo becomes a governed, monitored deployment, not just a working prototype.

  • The metric: the strongest customer stories name a number - deflection rate, resolution time - and how they proved it.

The hard questions to ask

These four questions cut through almost any Agentforce pitch:

  1. What did the data work take? Every real rollout involved data readiness. If a story skips it, you are seeing the highlight reel.

  2. How is the agent governed in production? Ask about monitoring, approvals for sensitive actions, and who owns the agent after launch.

  3. What did not work? The most useful answer at Dreamforce. A credible practitioner will tell you where agents struggled and why.

  4. How long from pilot to production? The real timeline, including foundational work, calibrates your own expectations fast.

WATCH FOR 'AGENT WASHING'
Gartner has warned that many vendors are rebranding chatbots and basic automation as agents. At Dreamforce, test the claim directly: ask what actions the agent takes autonomously and what data it acts on. If the answer is vague, it is probably an assistant wearing an agent costume.

The context to keep in mind

Agentforce is real - Salesforce reports it has passed $1 billion in ARR. But Gartner still expects over 40% of agentic projects to be cancelled by 2027, almost always for data, scope, and governance gaps rather than the AI. The demo is the easy part; the questions above are where production readiness lives.

seo_description: A practical framework to build the business case for Salesforce AI and Agentforce - the value levers, the metrics that persuade a CFO, and how to avoid vanity ROI.
body_html:
The hardest part of a Salesforce AI project is often not the technology; it is getting it funded. Leadership will not sign off on a demo. They will sign off on a business case that names a value lever, a baseline, and a credible number. Here is how to build that case, which metrics actually persuade a CFO, and how to avoid the vanity ROI that gets a project cancelled at its first review.

THE NUMBER THAT SHOULD SHAPE YOUR CASE
Gartner projects that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 , most for unclear business value rather than technical failure. A rigorous, measurable business case is the single best protection against being in that 40%. Source: Gartner

Anchor the case to a value lever, not a feature

A business case built on 'we will use AI' fails. A business case built on 'we will cut average handle time in service by X, worth Y' gets funded. Every credible Salesforce AI case begins by naming the lever it moves and the number attached to it.

Value lever

Where it shows up

Example metric

Cost to serve

Service, support ops

Case deflection rate, handle time

Revenue velocity

Sales

Cycle time, conversion, rep capacity

Retention

Service, success

Churn, CSAT, first-contact resolution

Productivity

Any team

Hours returned, tasks automated

Risk reduction

Compliance, ops

Errors avoided, SLA adherence

The four-step ROI framework

  1. Baseline the current state. Measure the metric today before anything changes. No baseline, no defensible ROI.

  2. Model a conservative improvement. Estimate the change, then halve your optimism. A conservative case that clears the bar beats an ambitious one that gets picked apart.

  3. Cost the whole effort honestly. Include implementation, data readiness, and change management, not just licensing. Under-costing is how projects blow their own ROI.

  4. Define the review checkpoint. Name when and how you will prove it worked. A case with a built-in measurement point survives scrutiny.

The metrics that actually move a CFO

Executives discount soft claims, so anchor the case in numbers they already trust:

  • Hard cost: reduction in cost to serve or hours of manual work removed.

  • Capacity: the same team handling more volume without hiring.

  • Speed: shorter cycle or resolution time, tied to revenue or retention.

  • Payback period: when the investment turns net positive - the number a CFO remembers.

One more discipline decides whether a funded case actually ships: feasibility. A high-value use case that is not feasible is a plan to spend money slowly. Score every candidate on value and feasibility - is the data ready, how complex is the build, how much change does it demand - so the case you fund is the one most likely to reach production. Our AI-powered business and data strategy teams exist precisely to make high-value cases feasible.

THE VANITY-ROI TRAP
The use case that draws the loudest applause is often the one with the least measurable value. Guard against it: make every candidate declare its owner and its metric before it competes for budget. Impressive is not the same as fundable.

Salesforce can run almost anything, which is exactly the problem for a mid-market buyer. Faced with a dozen clouds, add-ons, and AI options, many teams over-buy licenses they never fully use and under-invest in the data foundation that makes any of it work. This guide is deliberately opinionated: it tells you which clouds a mid-market company actually needs, where AI genuinely fits, and how to sequence the spend so value shows up early.

Start with the outcome, not the cloud

The most expensive mid-market mistake is buying a cloud because a competitor has it. Start instead with the two or three outcomes that matter this year - shorten sales cycles, deflect support volume, unify customer data - and let those pick the platform. If a product does not map to an outcome you can name, it is not on this year's list.

Where AI genuinely fits for a mid-market team

Agentforce changes the economics of automation because it runs on the platform you already own, so enterprise-grade capability no longer requires an enterprise-sized team. The catch is data readiness: an agent that cannot trust its data cannot be trusted to act. For a mid-market company that gets that right, capacity stops scaling with headcount and starts scaling with data and design - a genuine structural advantage over larger, slower competitors.

How to avoid over-buying

  • Buy for adoption, not aspiration. License what you will use in the next two quarters; you can expand, but you rarely claw back shelfware.

  • Fund the data foundation first. A clean, unified data layer makes every later investment work; skipping it is why AI stalls.

  • Phase the rollout. Prove value on one cloud or use case, then expand with the credibility it earns.

  • Right-size governance. You need control, not enterprise bureaucracy - design it to your scale from day one.

A sensible 12-month sequence

  1. Q1: stand up or clean up Sales Cloud and the core data model; fix data quality first.

  2. Q2: add Service Cloud and self-service; begin unifying data in Data Cloud.

  3. Q3: ship one Agentforce use case with clear guardrails and a metric.

  4. Q4: expand the agent, add analytics, and revisit which add-ons have earned their place.

The through-line: sequence for value, and let each phase fund the next. That discipline is what separates a mid-market Salesforce program that compounds from one that becomes expensive shelfware.

Ask a room of Salesforce leaders why their last project ran long, and almost none will blame the technology. They will describe discovery that started from a blank page, a data model argued over from scratch, integrations hand-built for the third time, and testing improvised at the end. BY THE NUMBERS

First, Define "Time-to-Value" - Because the Term Gets Abused

A 50% claim is meaningless without a definition, so here is ours. Time-to-value is the elapsed time from project kickoff to the first release that is live in production and delivering a measurable business outcome - not a demo, not a sandbox, not a go-live with a punch list a mile long. We measure to first production value because that is the moment the investment starts paying back. Everything before it is cost; everything after it is return. Accelerators are designed to shorten the cost side of that line.

Holding to that definition matters. It is easy to look fast by declaring victory at a demo. It is honest to measure the day a real user does real work and a real metric moves.

Why Programs Are Slow: The 80/20 of Delivery

Look closely at a slow Salesforce program and the delay is rarely in the differentiating 20% of the work - the logic and experiences that make your business distinct. It is in the foundational 80% that looks roughly the same across every implementation:

  • Discovery from a blank page - re-interviewing, re-documenting, and re-deciding patterns that are already well established.

  • Foundational data modeling from zero - rebuilding standard objects, relationships, and record structures most orgs share.

  • Integration plumbing, hand-built again - the same CRM, ERP, and billing connections, re-engineered per project.

  • Improvised testing and deployment - QA and release processes assembled late, under pressure.

  • Governance invented on the fly - readiness, security, and change management figured out mid-flight.

None of that is where your competitive advantage lives. It is necessary, but it is undifferentiated - and undifferentiated work is exactly what should be pre-solved.
